opus-5.5.text:
Even when you have the model weights, reproducing a result involves much more than the model. A published number is the output of a whole pipeline, and most of that pipeline is never fully documented.

The first problem is data. Papers will say "we fine-tuned on dataset X," but which version? How was it filtered and deduplicated? Was anything removed? Datasets scraped from the web change over time. Links rot and content gets taken down, so the dataset you download today may not be the one the authors used. With large pretraining corpora, you often can't get the data at all.

Then there are the many small decisions that never make it into the paper: hyperparameters, random seeds, learning rate schedules, the exact prompt template, how outputs were post-processed before scoring. With language models especially, small changes in prompt wording or formatting can shift benchmark scores a lot. Evaluation code itself is a big source of variation. Two groups can run "the same benchmark" and get different numbers because one normalizes answers differently or uses a different few-shot setup.

Hardware and software matter too. Different GPUs, library versions and CUDA kernels can produce slightly different numerical results. Some operations are non-deterministic by default, so even rerunning on the same machine doesn't always give you identical outputs.

And there's a cost dimension that I care a lot about. Even if everything were documented perfectly, many academic labs simply can't afford the compute to retrain or even fully evaluate these large models. So reproducibility becomes something only a handful of well-resourced organizations can actually do, which isn't great for science.

Finally, there are incentives. The field rewards new state-of-the-art results, not careful replication. Releasing clean, documented code and data takes time that isn't really rewarded. Model cards, data sheets and reproducibility checklists have helped, but we're still far from a culture where replication is treated as a normal part of the work.

r002.rationale: It lists random seeds among undocumented decisions, but does not state that an unreported seed can prevent reproduction when the model, data, and code are available.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention the ML Reproducibility Challenge or the outcomes of its replication attempts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's this assumption that if you have access to the model weights, you can just reproduce whatever number is in the paper, and in practice that's almost never how it goes. The model itself is only one piece of the pipeline. There's the exact version of the dataset, which may have been filtered or deduplicated in some way that's described in a footnote, if at all. There's the preprocessing, the tokenization, the prompt templates if you're doing evaluation on a language model, the decoding parameters, the random seeds. And then there's the whole software stack underneath: which version of PyTorch, which version of CUDA, what hardware you ran on. I've literally seen the same model give different results on different GPUs because of numerical precision differences. So you end up with this long chain of small decisions, and any one of them can shift your number by a point or two, which in a lot of benchmarks is the entire gap between "state of the art" and "nothing to see here."

The other thing is that a lot of this stuff isn't documented because the people doing the work don't think of it as a result. It's just what they did to get things running. The code that produced the table might be a Jupyter notebook that was modified fifteen times, and the version on GitHub is not the version that produced the final figure. And nobody's doing this maliciously, it's just that the incentives are all pointed at the paper, not at making sure someone else can get the same number six months later.

And then with the really big models, there's this additional layer where even if everything is documented perfectly, you may not have the compute to re-run it. So you're taking it on faith. I've spent weeks trying to reproduce results from papers I had every reason to trust, and ended up within a reasonable range but never exactly on the reported number. And I think that's actually the honest state of the field: we have a lot of results that are approximately reproducible, and we talk about them as if they were precisely reproducible. That's part of why I've pushed for things like model cards and dataset documentation, and for being more careful about what we're measuring when we measure things like energy use or carbon, because the same problems show up there too. If you don't record the hardware, the location, the duration, you can't compare anything.

astra-6.text:
Having access to the model is only one piece of the puzzle. You also need to know how the data was collected and processed, which version of the dataset was used, what the training setup was, and how the model was evaluated. A lot of those details don’t necessarily make it into a paper.

Even something as simple as a different random seed or a slightly different software version can affect the results. So you might have the code and the model and still struggle to get the same numbers, because you’re missing some of the choices that went into the experiment. That’s why documentation is so important: sharing the model is useful, but it doesn’t capture the whole process.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation details may be missing, but does not state that different evaluation procedures across language models make their reported results incomparable.

r002.rationale: It says a different random seed can affect results despite having the code and model, but does not clearly describe an unreported seed preventing reproduction when the training data is also available.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention the ML Reproducibility Challenge or the success rate of its replication attempts.
